visuals.title: Quiz
visuals.text: Ten questions across week four: Marco reads five, and five more are on the cards. Answer along, then hear Marco's answers.

quiz.pause_at: Pause here if you want to think it through

questions.q: Cost savings of 80 a year before tax, 25% tax, a 10% discount rate and no growth. What are they worth?
questions.explain: 80 × 75% = 60 after tax, ÷ 10% = 600. Skipping the tax gives 800.

questions.q: A buyer on 16x earnings buys a target at 20x, at the offer price, all in shares, no synergies. Accretive or dilutive?

options.text: Can't tell without the share count

questions.explain: The target yields 1 ÷ 20 = 5%, less than the 1 ÷ 16 ≈ 6.25% the buyer's shares cost, so earnings per share fall.

questions.q: A buyer pays 2,000. Book net assets are 500, write-ups 600, tax 25%. Goodwill?
questions.explain: 500 + 600 − 150 of deferred tax = 950 of fair value; 2,000 − 950 = 1,050. Price minus book value gives 1,500.

questions.q: An IPO sells 40 million shares at €15, 10 million of them new. How much does the company receive?
questions.explain: Only the new shares raise money for the company: 10m × €15 = €150m. The other €450m goes to the seller.
questions.explain_at: Third trap. The offer raises six hundred million

questions.q: Mobico's shares rose to about 39.5p against a 46p proposal. What is the gap telling you?

options.text: Doubt that a firm offer will come

questions.explain: The proposal is non-binding, so the market prices the risk that no firm offer arrives. Shares above the offer would signal a higher bid.
questions.explain_at: The gap between the share price and the offer is the market's view of the risk

questions.q: Bidder A offers 1,200 with a one in five chance its financing fails; Bidder B offers 1,000, fully financed. Which is worth more to the seller?

options.text: Bidder A, if it pays a fee

questions.explain: 80% × 1,200 = 960, below B's 1,000, before counting the damage a failed sale does to the business.

questions.q: A target is worth 2,000 on its own, net synergies are worth 600, and the buyer offers 2,400. How much of the synergies is paid away?
questions.explain: The premium is 400 out of 600 of synergies: two thirds. Paying the walk-away price of 2,600 would give away all of them.
questions.explain_at: How much of the synergies has it paid away

questions.q: Goodwill is impaired by 300, and the charge isn't tax deductible. What happens to cash?
questions.explain: The cash left when the company was bought. The impairment is non-cash and is added back on the cash flow statement.
questions.explain_at: Second trap. The value is gone

questions.q: Unaffected price €40, a leak takes the shares to €46, and the bidder offers €50. What's the premium?
questions.explain: 50 ÷ 40 − 1 = 25%. Measuring against the leaked €46 gives under 9%, a price that already contains the bid.

questions.q: Paying with debt instead of shares turns a dilutive deal accretive. What does that tell you?

options.text: Debt makes it a better-value deal
The financing changed, not the value
The target is worth more with debt

questions.explain: Same company, same price: only the cost of the money changed. Earnings per share doesn't see the extra risk the debt adds.
questions.explain_at: First trap. Same company, same price
